tagline: A thousand islands on a crescent coast
overview:
Croatia curves like a crescent moon around the northern Adriatic Sea and the western Balkans. Roughly the size of West Virginia, it has one of the most spectacular coastlines in Europe, with more than 1,200 islands, rocky coves, and walled medieval towns like Dubrovnik and Split. Inland, the capital, Zagreb, is a city of Austro-Hungarian avenues, red-tiled roofs, and busy cafés. Croatia borders Slovenia, Hungary, Serbia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, and Montenegro.

About 3.9 million people live here, and Croatian, written in the Latin alphabet, is the official language. Most Croats are Roman Catholic. Croatia became an independent country in 1991 as Yugoslavia broke apart, joined the European Union in 2013, and adopted the euro in 2023. It is a parliamentary republic. Tourism is the biggest industry, drawing millions of summer visitors to the beaches, and Croatians have punched far above their weight in sports, finishing second at the 2018 soccer World Cup with a population smaller than many cities.
landAndNature: Croatia has three very different regions. The long Dalmatian coast is a land of limestone, olive trees, lavender, and clear turquoise water, sheltered from the open sea by chains of islands such as Hvar, Brač, and Korčula. Behind the coast the Dinaric Alps rise steeply, with Dinara peak at 1,831 meters. Inland lie the flat, fertile plains of Slavonia along the Sava and Drava rivers. Plitvice Lakes National Park, a UNESCO site, features 16 lakes stepping down in terraces linked by waterfalls, colored startling shades of green and blue by minerals. Brown bears, wolves, and lynx live in the mountains, griffon vultures nest on Cres island, and Kopački Rit wetland teems with herons and storks. Summers are hot and dry on the coast, winters cold inland.
peopleAndCulture: Coastal life follows the sea: fishermen mend nets in harbors, and towns hold klapa singing sessions where groups of men harmonize without instruments, a tradition recognized by UNESCO. Food changes with the region, from grilled fish, black cuttlefish risotto, and pašticada beef stew on the coast to spicy kulen sausage and paprika-rich fish stews in Slavonia. The necktie was invented here, evolving from scarves Croatian soldiers wore in the 1600s. Sports are a national pride: Croatia's soccer team, in its red-and-white checkerboard shirts, reached two World Cup finals, and the country excels at water polo, handball, tennis, and basketball. Dubrovnik's old city hosts a summer festival of theater, and the inventor Nikola Tesla was born in the Croatian village of Smiljan.
history: Illyrians and Greeks lived on the coast before Rome took over; the emperor Diocletian built a huge palace at Split around the year 300 that people still live inside today. Croats, a Slavic people, arrived in the 600s and formed a kingdom by 925. From 1102 Croatia was joined to Hungary, and later to the Habsburg Empire, while Venice ruled much of the coast and Dubrovnik stayed a proud independent republic for centuries. After World War I Croatia became part of Yugoslavia. During World War II a Nazi-backed regime committed atrocities. Croatia declared independence from Yugoslavia in 1991, and a war followed until 1995, destroying towns like Vukovar and killing thousands. The country joined NATO in 2009 and the European Union in 2013.
funFacts: The necktie descends from the cravat worn by Croatian soldiers in the 1600s; Croatia celebrates Cravat Day every October 18.
Croatia has more than 1,200 islands, islets, and rocks, but only about 50 of them are inhabited.
Diocletian's Palace in Split is a 1,700-year-old Roman palace that still contains homes, shops, and cafés.
Croatian inventor Nikola Tesla developed the alternating-current electricity system used in homes worldwide.
The Sea Organ in Zadar is a set of pipes under stone steps that plays musical notes as waves push air through them.
